elusive

/ih-LOO-siv/ — stress on LOO · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something elusive is difficult to find, catch, or pin down.

The perfect paper airplane design remained elusive despite forty-seven attempts.

Example

The answer to the riddle was elusive; the more she thought about it, the more it slipped away.

Elude (slip away) + -ive (inclined to): the answer has the quality of slipping away from grasp. More precise than 'difficult' because elusive captures the sense of something that dodges capture.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

obscure: Obscure means hard to see or understand because it is dim, little known, or buried in complexity — an obscure reference, an obscure rule. Elusive adds pursuit: you are actively hunting the thing, and it keeps slipping away. Obscure sits in shadow; elusive escapes the hand reaching for it.

slippery: Slippery is the informal cousin: a slippery idea or slippery character is hard to hold onto and maybe not to be trusted. Elusive is more neutral and more formal — it says only that the thing keeps escaping your search, with no hint of dishonesty attached.

intangible: Intangible means unable to be touched or physically grasped at all — hope and reputation are intangible by nature. Elusive things may be perfectly solid, like a mouse in the walls; they are just hard to find or catch. Intangible is what a thing is; elusive is how it behaves.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

obvious: easily seen or understood at once

attainable: able to be reached or caught

Where it sits · how actively it slips out of reach

rare → fleeting → evasive → elusive

rare vs. elusive: Something rare is merely hard to come across; something elusive seems to actively slip out of reach.

fleeting vs. elusive: A fleeting sight vanishes quickly, but an elusive one can barely be caught in the first place.

evasive vs. elusive: 'Evasive' describes deliberately dodging, while elusive is the ultimate escape — nearly impossible to find, catch, or pin down.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — elus-: shifted stem of elude — from Latin eludere, 'to slip away, play off' (root ludere, 'to play') (Latin)

Suffix — -ive: having the quality or tendency of (Latin)

Put it together: Elude swaps its -de ending for -s- before -ive: inclined to slip away — hard to find, catch, or pin down. Sound-alike alert: allusive (making indirect references) is a completely different word.

Use the root in a new word: elude: The clever fox managed to elude the hounds by doubling back through the stream.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal

Reach for elusive when something you're trying to find, catch, or understand keeps slipping away despite effort. Use it for abstract things (answers, memories, goals) as well as physical ones.
